reference.source: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology / Oxford Handbook of Nephrology and Hypertension
clinicalPearls: C3 glomerulopathy is defined by glomerular deposition of complement C3 with little or no immunoglobulin on immunofluorescence, reflecting dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway
It encompasses two entities distinguished on electron microscopy: dense deposit disease, with dense intramembranous deposits, and C3 glomerulonephritis, with subendothelial and mesangial deposits
Presentation ranges from asymptomatic haematuria or proteinuria to nephrotic syndrome or a nephritic picture, often with low serum C3 and a normal C4
An acquired autoantibody, the C3 nephritic factor, stabilises the alternative-pathway C3 convertase and perpetuates complement consumption in many patients
Inherited or acquired abnormalities of complement regulators (such as factor H) or activators can underlie the disease
Diagnosis rests on kidney biopsy with immunofluorescence and electron microscopy, supported by a complement functional and genetic workup
Management combines general glomerular disease measures with immunosuppression in some cases; complement-targeted therapy is used in selected or refractory disease
Dense deposit disease may be associated with retinal drusen and acquired partial lipodystrophy
reference.pathophysiology: C3 glomerulopathy results from persistent activation and dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway in the fluid phase, leading to deposition of C3 breakdown products within the glomerulus. Normally the alternative-pathway C3 convertase is tightly regulated by proteins such as factor H and factor I; in this disease acquired autoantibodies (notably C3 nephritic factor, which stabilises the convertase) or genetic abnormalities in complement regulators or activators allow uncontrolled convertase activity and continuous C3 turnover. The resulting C3 fragments accumulate along the glomerular basement membrane and mesangium, producing the characteristic complement-dominant, immunoglobulin-poor staining. This drives glomerular inflammation and a membranoproliferative pattern of injury, manifesting clinically as haematuria, proteinuria and progressive loss of kidney function, with correspondingly low circulating C3.
additionalDifferentials: Atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome (also complement-mediated but a thrombotic microangiopathy)
additionalInvestigations: Kidney biopsy with immunofluorescence (C3-dominant staining) and electron microscopy to subclassify
Serum complement (low C3 with normal C4 typical of alternative-pathway activation)
Complement functional assays and detection of C3 nephritic factor and other autoantibodies
Assessment of complement regulator levels (e.g. factor H) and terminal complement activity
Screening for monoclonal gammopathy, especially in older adults
Genetic testing of alternative-pathway complement genes
redFlags: Nephrotic-range proteinuria with declining renal function
reference.prognosis: C3 glomerulopathy is frequently progressive, with a substantial proportion of patients reaching end-stage kidney disease over years, and it commonly recurs after transplantation; outcome varies with histological severity and the underlying complement abnormality.
pitfalls: Misclassifying it as immune-complex membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis without careful immunofluorescence
Overlooking an underlying monoclonal gammopathy driving complement dysregulation in older patients
Failing to perform a complement functional and genetic workup once the biopsy pattern is recognised
Not anticipating disease recurrence in the allograft
Confusing it with atypical HUS, which shares complement dysregulation but presents as thrombotic microangiopathy
references: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology (Feehally, Floege, Tonelli, Johnson)
KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases
management: Reduce proteinuria and control blood pressure with renin-angiotensin system blockade as baseline nephroprotective therapy.
Offer immunosuppression, typically corticosteroids with mycophenolate mofetil, for progressive or moderate-to-severe disease.
Consider terminal complement inhibition with eculizumab in rapidly progressive or treatment-resistant disease showing terminal-pathway activation.
Identify and treat any underlying driver, including clone-directed therapy where a monoclonal gammopathy is causal.
Monitor renal function, proteinuria and serum complement to track disease activity and treatment response.
Involve nephrology and plan transplantation with awareness of the high risk of post-transplant recurrence.
Arrange complement functional and genetic testing with counselling, and screen for inherited regulator defects.
